issues.issue: Eligibility here requires only presence on the Group I list "effective the date of ratification," whereas paragraph 3.A(2) defines Eligible Group I Employees as those on the list at signing who remain on it at ratification. Someone added between the two dates qualifies under one test and not the other.
"Interest at prevailing market interest rates" is left without index, measurement date or method. The annuity's value therefore turns on an unspecified term.

Guaranteed Employees are "those Regular Situation Holders to be identified on Attachments '1' and '2'", but no such attachments appear in the instrument and the phrase "to be identified" leaves the class to be fixed later. Who is a Guaranteed Employee cannot be determined from the document.

"Guaranteed the opportunity to work five straight time shifts per week" promises an opportunity rather than pay or work, and "duration of their guarantee period" is defined elsewhere. What the employer must actually provide is arguable.

The guarantee of five shifts sits against Appendix A.C, which lets The Times utilize Guaranteed Employees in inverse seniority order, and Appendix A.E, which suspends the guarantee in stated circumstances. Reconciling the promise with those limits is a genuine question.

The Attachment 1 guarantee "shall survive the expiration of this Agreement," which is hard to square with the Memorandum's term ending March 30, 2000 and with the Appendix A.E provisions terminating guarantees. The duration of a surviving guarantee would have to be construed.

The guarantee runs "until the expiration date of the current Collective Bargaining Agreement," but the Memorandum both describes the current CBA as expiring March 30, 1993 and extends it to March 30, 2000. "Current Collective Bargaining Agreement" is genuinely ambiguous as to which date is meant.

"Utilize fully the services of Guaranteed Employees ... in inverse seniority order" does not say whether inverse seniority governs assignment among guaranteed employees or the order of exhausting them. The two readings produce opposite work assignments.

The exception for "Eligible Group I Employees who obtain guarantees pursuant to paragraph 4B" depends on paragraph 4.B, which speaks of a guarantee "governed by the terms of Appendix A" without identifying which Attachment's terms apply. The scope of those add-on guarantees is unresolved.

Suspension turns on the delivery department's operations being suspended "in circumstances under which RSH's are not entitled to be paid under the Collective Bargaining Agreement," a condition that depends on an unquoted external document. Whether a given shutdown qualifies is open.

"Permanent suspension of the Newspaper" is undefined and could mean cessation of publication entirely or of a particular edition or operation. The trigger for ending all guarantees rests on that phrase.

"Terminates employment for any reason, including but not limited to, retirement, resignation, discharge, death and permanent disability" mixes voluntary and involuntary events under a verb implying employee choice. Whether an employer discharge defeats the guarantee is exactly the tension between the general phrase and the enumerated items.

Termination of guarantees requires a violation continuing after a court's temporary restraining order, while paragraph 7.C releases a party from the no-strike clause in defined circumstances. Whether a permitted 7.C work stoppage is a "violation of that No-Strike clause" here is unresolved.

The me-too right depends on undefined terms — a "wage package which is additional to or different from that contained herein," wages "granted in exchange for productivity improvements or attrition exceeding" the NMDU deal, and wages "diverted from an existing or subsequently negotiated wage package." Each condition is vague and would have to be construed to apply the clause.

"The 43rd Street and/or the staging facility" uses "and/or" and an unidentified "staging facility," so the excluded premises are not fixed. The exclusion's boundary is the kind of term parties dispute.

This carve-out cuts across paragraph 1.A, which applies the contract as modified "at any new or rebuilt facility," and against the Carlstadt letter contemplating transfers to 43rd Street. Which regime governs 43rd Street is a live question.

Freezing the forty current finishing times "throughout the duration of this contract" conflicts with paragraph 6, which makes the SNBD reorganization "subject only to" a forty-route minimum, and with the 4:00 p.m. start-time provision. The three cannot obviously be applied together.

Funding shortfalls out of paragraph 3.A(3) contributions is hard to square with 3.A(3) itself, which caps the obligation at a 450-FTE minimum and declares those contributions "in lieu of and not in addition to" other contributions. The extent of any additional Times obligation is a genuine construction issue.

"Shift contributions needed to maintain benefit status" is a standard set by the Fund's own rules rather than by this document, so the amount owed is undefined here. What triggers and measures the shortfall is open.

The condition is the individuals' "willingness ... to avail themselves of all work opportunities that may exist at The New York Times," a subjective and unbounded standard. Whether a refusal of some work defeats funding for all is unresolved.

The increase runs only "during the period between ratification and the full commencement of operations at Edison," a terminal event with no defined date. When the enhanced FTE obligation stops is uncertain.

This letter raises the paragraph 3-A(3) minimum above 450 FTEs while the 1996 letter reduces it, so the actual annual contribution obligation is the resultant of three inconsistent instruments. Harmonising them is a real question.
"Every effort within its control" is an unmeasured standard and "hootlegging" is put in scare quotes without definition. Both would have to be construed before the promise could be enforced.
The committee is "charged with administering the transfer process" without any stated decision rule for a two-two committee or any substantive transfer criteria. Its authority is undefined.

The 1996 contributions are to be offset by reductions "evenly distributed throughout the calendar years 1992, 1993, 1994, and 1995," i.e. reductions in earlier years for contributions not yet made. The mechanism is internally illogical as written.

The reduction cuts into the 450-FTE annual minimum guaranteed by paragraph 3-A(3), and the FTE side letter simultaneously increases that minimum. What the Times actually owes for 1992-1995 cannot be read off any one of them.

"On an inverse seniority basis, to assign the most junior qualified situation holder" leaves "qualified" undefined and the pool of situation holders unspecified. The clause also uses "any such situations" without an antecedent in the quoted text.

The volunteer procedure is to be followed "prior to instituting the procedure above," yet the preceding paragraphs already provide for immediate junior assignment pending final award. The order of operations between the two paragraphs is inconsistent.

"Foreseen to be of two (2) weeks or less duration" gives no indication of who forms the forecast or when, and a vacancy that outlasts the forecast is unaddressed. The exception's application is uncertain.

An unqualified "option to fill" the resulting vacancy sits against the preceding paragraphs' mandatory notice, volunteer and restoration procedures for filling situations. Whether the option escapes those procedures is arguable.

The NMDU "may, within 72 hours, discuss the possibility of employment opportunities," which promises nothing beyond a conversation and starts an unexplained 72-hour clock. Whether any obligation arises at all is the question.
